strengths: Important Problem: The paper investigates a critical and pervasive failure mode in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models—namely, the 'vision shortcut' where policies trained on goal-driven datasets ignore language instructions and overfit to visual correlations.

Insightful Motivational Analysis: Section 2 provides compelling pilot experiments across RoboCasa, LIBERO, and SimplerEnv demonstrating that vision-only policies often perform on par with language-conditioned policies in-distribution, yet collapse in ambiguous or out-of-distribution environments.

Decoupled Action Interface: The use of Latent Action Queries as a bottleneck interface between the VLM backbone and the Diffusion Transformer action head is computationally efficient, reducing DiT conditioning complexity from $O(N^2)$ to $O(K^2)$ without test-time inference overhead.
Empirical Gains: On SimplerEnv and RoboCasa, the proposed approach shows notable improvements in success rates compared to the QwenGR00T base framework.
weaknesses: Fundamental Conceptual Disconnect in Objective Formulation: The entire theoretical motivation is grounded on maximizing the conditional Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) between actions $a$ and instructions $\ell$ given visual context $v$, which requires computing or estimating $\log p(\ell \mid a, v) - \log p(\ell \mid v)$ (Eq. 4 and Appendix A). However, in the actual implementation (Eq. 7), the likelihood is computed as $\log p(\ell \mid v, H_Q^{\text{prior}})$. In the Priori Branch ($[v, Q, \ell]$ with causal masking), $H_Q^{\text{prior}}$ attends exclusively to $v$ and has no access to the ground-truth action $a$. Thus, $H_Q^{\text{prior}}$ is strictly a function of visual observation $v$, meaning that Eq. (7) does not condition on $a$ at all. Instead, it effectively amounts to predicting $\ell$ from $v$ through intermediate bottleneck tokens, which directly contradicts the stated goal of computing the mutual information between language and action.

Contradiction Regarding the Vision Shortcut: The authors argue that in goal-driven datasets, $p(\ell \mid v)$ is sharp and enables visual shortcuts. Yet, Eq. (7) explicitly trains the model to maximize the language generation likelihood of $\ell$ given $v$ and $Q$ (where $Q$ only sees $v$). Rewarding the model for predicting language from visual cues reinforces rather than penalizes the visual correlation $v \to \ell$.

Severe Discrepancy Between Main Results and Ablations: In Table 1, BayesianVLA + Qwen3-VL-4B is reported to achieve success rates of 89.6%, 63.8%, 33.3%, and 79.2% across the four SimplerEnv tasks, averaging 66.5%. However, in Table 3 (the ablation study using the exact same backbone and benchmark), BayesianVLA is reported with completely different numbers: 81.9%, 66.6%, 34.7%, and 70.8%, averaging 63.5%. The manuscript provides no explanation for this significant divergence.

Unfulfilled Experimental Claims and Inconsistent Writing: The opening of Section 4 explicitly states that experiments are conducted on four simulation benchmarks: SimplerEnv, LIBERO, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin2. However, RoboTwin2 does not appear anywhere in the paper, and LIBERO is only used in the motivational section (Section 2) rather than as a benchmark evaluation for BayesianVLA. In fact, the 'Limitation and Future Work' section on page 12 explicitly admits: 'We plan to extend our experimental validation to include the RoboTwin and LIBERO benchmarks', directly contradicting the claim in Section 4.

Confounded Explanation for Retaining Text Capabilities: Section 4.3 attributes the preservation of conversational abilities in BayesianVLA to the Bayesian decomposition. However, standard VLA models (such as QwenGR00T) are fine-tuned purely with action regression/diffusion losses, naturally suffering from catastrophic forgetting of language generation. In contrast, BayesianVLA optimizes an auxiliary language modeling loss on $\ell$ (Eq. 7). The preservation of text capabilities is a well-known consequence of multi-tasking with an autoregressive language modeling objective rather than an emergent benefit of Bayesian policy decomposition.

strengths: Relevant and timely problem: Addressing the 'vision shortcut' / instruction-ignoring pathology in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models trained on goal-driven manipulation datasets is an important and recognized challenge in embodied AI.

Insightful motivational experiments: The pilot evaluations in Section 2 (demonstrating high performance of vision-only policies in ID settings and severe drops in ambiguous settings like LIBERO Goal) effectively illustrate the reliance of standard models on visual shortcuts.

Architectural efficiency: Employing Latent Action Queries to decouple the context length of the VLM from the Diffusion Transformer policy is an appealing architectural inductive bias that reduces cross-attention complexity.
weaknesses: Fundamental theoretical and formulation disconnect: The paper motivates the method by maximizing the conditional Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) / Log-Likelihood Ratio (LLR) between action and instruction, formulated in Eq. (4) as log p(l | a, v) - log p(l | v). However, in Eq. (7), this is instantiated as L_LLR = log p(l | v, H_Q^prior) - sg(log p(l | v)). This has several severe mathematical flaws: (1) Actions (either ground truth a or policy-generated a) do not appear in Eq. (7) or in the computation of H_Q^prior. (2) Due to causal masking in the Priori branch ([v, Q, l]), H_Q^prior is strictly a function of v alone. By the data processing inequality, I(l; H_Q^prior | v) = 0; H_Q^prior cannot provide any mutual information about l beyond v. (3) The DiT parameters psi do not receive any gradient from L_LLR in Eq. (9). As a result, L_LLR is simply an auxiliary language modeling objective predicting instruction l from vision v with soft prefix prompts Q. It does not penalize vision shortcuts or optimize mutual information between actions and instructions.

Contradictory and unfulfilled experimental claims: In Section 4, the manuscript states: 'we conducted extensive experiments on four simulation benchmarks: SimplerEnv, LIBERO, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin2.' However, the paper only reports results on SimplerEnv and RoboCasa. In Section 5 ('Limitation and Future Work'), the text contradicts itself, stating: 'We plan to extend our experimental validation to include the RoboTwin and LIBERO benchmarks'. Claiming benchmarks in the main experimental setup that were not actually conducted or included indicates an incomplete submission.

Severe data discrepancies and reporting errors: In Table 1, BayesianVLA + Qwen3-VL-4B is reported to achieve an average of 66.5% on SimplerEnv (89.6%, 63.8%, 33.3%, 79.2%). However, in Table 3 (Ablation study on the exact same benchmark and backbone), BayesianVLA is reported with completely different numbers: average 63.5% (81.9%, 66.6%, 34.7%, 70.8%). There is no explanation for why the full method has different scores across tables. Additionally, in Table 1, the QwenGR00T baseline shows an Eggplant success rate of 64.2%, but the column average (55.2%) only mathematically matches an Eggplant value of 54.2% (as listed in Table 3).

Misattribution of conversational capability preservation: Section 4.3 attributes the preservation of text generation (Figures 4 and 5) to the Bayesian decomposition overcoming vision shortcuts. In reality, standard VLA baselines degenerate because they are fine-tuned purely on regression/diffusion action loss without any language modeling objective. BayesianVLA adds an explicit next-token cross-entropy loss on instruction text via Eq. (7), which naturally preserves text generation. Attributing this to Bayesian grounding of actions is misleading.

Marginal improvement on RoboCasa: On RoboCasa (Table 2), BayesianVLA achieves 50.4%, compared to 48.8% for QwenOFT and 47.8% for QwenGR00T. With only 50 trials per task, the standard error across tasks is around 1.4-1.5%, making the +1.6% to +2.6% gain statistically marginal.

strengths: Relevant and timely research focus: The paper targets an important pathology in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models—the 'vision shortcut'—where policies trained on goal-driven manipulation datasets overfit to visual correlations and ignore language instructions.

Insightful motivating experiments: The diagnostic experiments in Section 2 effectively demonstrate that vision-only policies perform competitively on standard in-distribution benchmarks (e.g., 44.6% vs 47.8% on RoboCasa), clearly exposing the extent of visual bias present in current manipulation datasets.

Latent Action Query bottleneck: Using dedicated action query tokens to condition the continuous Diffusion Transformer policy is an effective architectural choice that decouples diffusion head conditioning complexity from the full visual-language token sequence length.
weaknesses: Fundamental conceptual disconnect in the core objective: The theoretical derivation relies on maximizing the conditional Pointwise Mutual Information between action $a$ and instruction $\ell$, given vision $v$: $\text{PMI}(a, \ell \mid v) = \log p(\ell \mid a, v) - \log p(\ell \mid v)$. However, in the implementation (Eq. 7), $p(\ell \mid a, v)$ is replaced with $p(\ell \mid v, H_Q^{\text{prior}})$. Since $H_Q^{\text{prior}}$ is computed strictly from $[v, Q]$ via causal masking and never observes the ground-truth action trajectory $a$, $H_Q^{\text{prior}}$ is conditionally independent of $\ell$ given $v$. By the data processing inequality, $I(\ell; H_Q^{\text{prior}} \mid v) = 0$. The ground-truth action $a$ never appears in $\mathcal{L}_{\text{LLR}}$, invalidating the claim that this term explicitly rewards actions that explain the language command.

Unfulfilled and contradictory experimental claims: Section 4 states, 'we conducted extensive experiments on four simulation benchmarks: SimplerEnv, LIBERO, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin2.' However, the manuscript only provides evaluation results on SimplerEnv and RoboCasa. RoboTwin2 is absent entirely, and LIBERO is only used for the preliminary pilot study on the baseline. Furthermore, Section 'Limitation and Future Work' explicitly contradicts Section 4 by admitting: 'We plan to extend our experimental validation to include the RoboTwin and LIBERO benchmarks.'

Internal data inconsistency between tables: In Table 1, BayesianVLA + Qwen3-VL-4B is reported to achieve a 66.5% average success rate on SimplerEnv (89.6%, 63.8%, 33.3%, 79.2%). However, in Table 3 (the SimplerEnv ablation using the exact same Qwen3-VL-4B backbone), BayesianVLA is reported with an average of 63.5% (81.9%, 66.6%, 34.7%, 70.8%). No explanation is provided for this substantial discrepancy.

Modest improvements on RoboCasa and absence of real-world trials: On the RoboCasa benchmark (Table 2), BayesianVLA improves over the baseline by only 2.6% (50.4% vs 47.8%), while a Vision-Only model already scores 44.7% (and outperforms BayesianVLA on multiple individual tasks). In addition, no real-world robot evaluations are provided to substantiate real-world robustness.

Purely anecdotal evaluation of general capabilities: The claim that BayesianVLA prevents catastrophic forgetting of general VLM reasoning abilities is supported solely by two cherry-picked qualitative text-only examples in Figures 4 and 5, without standard quantitative evaluation on established language or vision-language benchmarks.

strengths: Important problem focus: The paper tackles a widespread failure mode in vision-language-action (VLA) models—the 'vision shortcut'—where policies overfit to correlations between scenes and actions, effectively ignoring language instructions.

Well-structured motivation: Section 2 provides compelling pilot experiments across three settings (in-distribution RoboCasa, ambiguous LIBERO-Goal, and out-of-distribution SimplerEnv) illustrating that vision-only baselines can match language-conditioned models when scenes deterministically map to tasks.

Comprehensive empirical scope: The framework is evaluated across standard simulation benchmarks (SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, LIBERO) and supplemented with real-world Franka robot experiments on colored blocks and vegetables.

Architectural efficiency at inference: Using Latent Action Queries to decouple the VLM context length from the action decoder ensures that no computational overhead is added at inference time compared to standard VLA models.
weaknesses: Fundamental mathematical and conceptual disconnect in the Bayesian formulation: The entire theoretical motivation rests on maximizing the log-likelihood ratio LLR = log p(l | a, v) - log p(l | v). However, in the proposed implementation (Eq. 7 and Section 3.3), the model evaluates log p(l | v, H^prior_Q) - sg(log p(l | v)). In the Priori Branch, the input sequence is [v, Q, l], where Q only attends to visual tokens v due to causal masking. Ground-truth action trajectory 'a' is never passed as an input to Q or to the VLM. Thus, H^prior_Q is purely a function of v, and log p(l | v, H^prior_Q) represents predicting language from visual features, not conditioning on action 'a'. The claim that 'Q encodes action information a (via the prior)' is invalid because Q is not conditioned on actions, meaning the model does not estimate p(l | a, v).

Self-contradictory objective: A core claim of the paper is that optimizing scene-to-instruction prediction p(l | v) causes information collapse and reinforces the vision shortcut (Section 2.4 and Table 10). Yet, maximizing Eq. (7) explicitly rewards the VLM for predicting instruction l from visual features [v, Q], which directly conflicts with the paper's premise that predicting l from v degrades language grounding.

Internal data and text discrepancies: There are multiple contradictions in reporting key numbers across the manuscript. On page 2 (Section 1, bullet 3), the authors report 'a remarkable 8.8% improvement in OOD generalization on SimplerEnv', whereas the Abstract and Section 4.1 report '11.3%'. In Section 4.5, the text states 'Comparing the full LangForce (63.5%) with the "+ Action Query" ablation (57.5%), we observe a significant performance boost (+6.0%)', whereas Table 1 and Table 5 report LangForce at 66.5% (+9.0%).

Unsubstantiated claims regarding preservation of general capabilities: Figures 4 and 5 claim that standard VLA fine-tuning degrades the VLM into repeating gibberish (e.g., 'Dentistate Dentistate...'), while LangForce preserves flawless, multi-step LaTeX mathematical reasoning. Fine-tuning a 4B VLM solely on robotic trajectories without general multimodal/math co-training while retaining complex zero-shot mathematical reasoning is implausible and contradicts known catastrophic forgetting dynamics. The paper lacks crucial training details (e.g., which layers of Qwen3-VL are frozen/tuned, whether LoRA or full parameter tuning is used) to substantiate this phenomenon.

strengths: Compelling Motivation and Problem Formulation: The paper addresses a prevalent yet often overlooked pathology in vision-language-action (VLA) training—the 'vision shortcut' or information collapse, where policies ignore language instructions because visual scenes in goal-driven datasets deterministically correlate with specific tasks. The motivational pilot experiments (in-distribution vs. LIBERO Goal and OOD SimplerEnv) clearly and convincingly illustrate this failure mode.

Clever Architectural Design via Latent Action Queries: By introducing learnable Latent Action Queries and exploiting the causal masking of decoder-only VLMs, the method elegantly instantiates both a vision-only prior branch ([v, Q, l]) and a language-conditioned posterior branch ([v, l, Q]) within a single shared model, avoiding clumsy multi-stage training pipelines.

Strong Empirical Results on Challenging Generalization Benchmarks: LangForce achieves substantial improvements where language disambiguation is crucial, notably achieving a +11.3% boost over the direct QwenGR00T baseline on the out-of-distribution SimplerEnv benchmark (66.5% vs. 55.2%) and resolving ambiguity in the LIBERO Goal suite (99.4% vs. 97.4%).

Real-World Validation and Preservation of General VLM Abilities: The authors validate the method on physical Franka manipulation across multi-object and vegetable pick-and-place tasks. Furthermore, Section 4.4 and Appendix B.4 provide an insightful analysis showing that the training objective helps prevent catastrophic forgetting of base conversational/reasoning capabilities.
weaknesses: Mathematical Disconnect Between Bayesian Formulation and the Practical Objective: In Section 3.1, Eq. (4) derives the log-likelihood ratio (LLR) as log p(l | a, v) - log p(l | v) = log [pi(a | v, l) / p(a | v)], which theoretically depends on the action variable a. However, in the implemented loss (Eq. 7), the likelihood is approximated as log p(l | v, H_Q^prior) without any explicit conditioning on the action a. Crucially, the authors note in Section 3.3 that H_Q^prior is detached when optimizing the flow-matching prior loss L_prior, meaning H_Q^prior does not receive action-supervision gradients and functions purely as an intermediate visual feature of v. The paper lacks a rigorous mathematical justification for why log p(l | v, H_Q^prior) serves as a valid surrogate for log p(l | a, v).

Lack of Wall-Clock Training Overhead Profiling: Although the authors note in Section 7 that inference overhead is zero and suggest a prefix prefill strategy for the identical vision prefix, training requires processing two branches with different token ordering ([v, Q, l] vs. [v, l, Q]). The manuscript does not report concrete empirical wall-clock training times, GPU memory consumption, or throughput comparisons relative to standard single-branch VLA fine-tuning.

Limited Evaluation on Contact-Rich Manipulation: As acknowledged in the limitations, both the simulation and real-world evaluations primarily focus on pick-and-place and spatial reach-to-receptacle setups. While these tasks are well-suited for measuring semantic instruction disambiguation, evaluating on contact-rich, highly dexterous manipulation tasks would strengthen the generalizability claims.

strengths: Compelling problem motivation: The paper investigates a prevalent failure mode in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models—the 'vision shortcut' / information collapse—where models exploit spurious scene-action correlations in goal-deterministic datasets and ignore language commands. The pilot experiments in Section 2 (demonstrating near-matching performance of vision-only models on single-task scenes, but catastrophic collapse on ambiguous scenes in LIBERO Goal and OOD SimplerEnv) provide clear and convincing empirical support for the problem.

Architectural efficiency via Latent Action Queries: Using K=64 learnable query tokens as an information bottleneck between the VLM backbone and the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) decouples the DiT cross-attention complexity from the length of visual and language context tokens (reducing DiT conditioning complexity from O(N^2) to O(K^2)), which is an effective architectural improvement.

Comprehensive empirical evaluations: The proposed framework is evaluated across multiple established benchmarks (SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, LIBERO) as well as physical robot experiments on a Franka Research 3 arm (multi-object pick-and-place with distractors and unseen colors, and vegetable pick-and-place). The empirical performance gains over the baseline QwenGR00T across these tasks are consistent.

Mitigation of catastrophic forgetting: The paper shows that incorporating language prediction objectives within the VLM backbone helps retain general conversational and reasoning capabilities that are otherwise degraded during standard VLA fine-tuning.
weaknesses: Fundamental theoretical disconnect between the Bayesian derivation and the objective implementation: The core conceptual foundation of the paper is maximizing the conditional Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) between action a and instruction ℓ given observation v, formulated as L_LLR = log (π(a | v, ℓ) / p(a | v)) = log p(ℓ | a, v) - log p(ℓ | v) (Eq. 4). However, in Eq. (7), this is implemented as L_LLR = log p(ℓ | v, H^prior_Q) - sg(log p(ℓ | v)), under the claim that 'Q encodes the action information a (via the prior)'. By construction, in the Priori branch Input_prior = [v, Q, ℓ], Q attends only to v due to causal masking, and the ground-truth action a is never fed into Q or the VLM. Furthermore, H^prior_Q is explicitly detached from L_prior, so no action gradients flow into H^prior_Q. Thus, H^prior_Q is strictly a deterministic function of v alone. By the Data Processing Inequality, I(ℓ; H^prior_Q | v) = 0, meaning H^prior_Q cannot mathematically provide any information about ℓ beyond what is already in v. Crucially, neither the action a nor the posterior policy π(a | v, ℓ) appears anywhere in L_LLR. As a result, L_LLR does not penalize policy collapse or estimate conditional PMI; it simply acts as an auxiliary visual captioning / instruction reconstruction loss.

Internal inconsistencies in quantitative results and manuscript text: There are multiple contradictory metrics across different sections. In Contribution 3 (page 2), the paper claims a 'remarkable 8.8% improvement in OOD generalization on SimplerEnv', whereas the Abstract and Section 4.1 state an '11.3% improvement' (66.5% vs. 55.2%). Furthermore, in Section 4.5 (Ablation Studies), the text states: 'Comparing the full LangForce (63.5%) with the "+ Action Query" ablation (57.5%), we observe a significant performance boost (+6.0%)', whereas Table 1 and Table 5 list full LangForce at 66.5% (+9.0% over 57.5%). These discrepancies suggest unverified text carried over from preliminary runs.

Ambiguity in gradient flow and training mechanics: In Section 3.3, the authors state that H^prior_Q is detached when optimizing L_prior to prevent the VLM backbone from learning visual shortcuts. However, if H^prior_Q is detached from the action loss and only receives gradients from L_LLR (which predicts ℓ from v), it is unclear how the VLM backbone learns any prior action distribution p(a | v). A formal computational graph or detailed parameter gradient specification is necessary to verify what each component actually learns.

Limited physical manipulation complexity: While the inclusion of real-robot evaluations is appreciated, the tasks remain restricted to tabletop pick-and-place with top-down grasping. Evaluating tasks involving richer contact dynamics, articulated object interactions, or multi-stage dexterous behaviors on the physical setup would provide stronger validation of the policy's real-world generalization.
